questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old male is admitted with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea. He is orthostatic and his mucous membranes are dry. Investigations show serum creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), BUN 56 mg/dL, urine sodium 8 mEq/L, and urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely type of acute kidney injury in this patient?

options.A: Intrinsic renal AKI due to acute tubular necrosis
options.B: Post-renal AKI due to urinary obstruction
options.C: Pre-renal AKI due to volume depletion
options.D: Intrinsic renal AKI due to acute interstitial nephritis

questions.explanation: This patient has classic pre-renal AKI. Key features include a history of volume loss (vomiting/diarrhea), low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L) indicating avid tubular sodium reabsorption, high urine osmolality (>500 mOsm/kg) indicating intact tubular concentrating ability, and an elevated BUN:Creatinine ratio (>20:1). The kidneys are functionally intact but underperfused. Prompt IV fluid resuscitation is the treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male with known CKD stage 5 presents with confusion, asterixis, and pericardial friction rub. His serum potassium is 6.8 mEq/L and bicarbonate is 10 mEq/L, refractory to medical management. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate infusion and dietary potassium restriction
options.C: Peritoneal dialysis catheter insertion and elective dialysis next week
options.D: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate and loop diuretics

questions.explanation: The AEIOU mnemonic defines absolute indications for urgent hemodialysis: Acidosis (refractory), Electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalemia refractory to treatment), Intoxication, Overload (fluid, refractory), and Uremia (encephalopathy, pericarditis). This patient has uremic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis), uremic pericarditis (friction rub), refractory hyperkalemia, and severe metabolic acidosis — meeting multiple absolute indications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with periorbital puffiness worse in the morning and progressively worsening bilateral pedal edema. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria with no hematuria. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL, cholesterol is 320 mg/dL, and 24-hour urine protein is 52 mg/kg/day. Renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy but effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: This child has Minimal Change Disease (MCD), the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (>80%). The classic tetrad is present: massive proteinuria (>40 mg/m²/hr or >3.5 g/day in adults), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. Biopsy shows normal light microscopy with podocyte foot process effacement on EM. First-line treatment is oral prednisolone (60 mg/m²/day for 4-6 weeks). ~90% of children respond completely.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female with Sjögren syndrome presents with generalized muscle weakness. ABG shows: pH 7.28, pCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L. Urine pH is 6.5 despite systemic acidosis. Urine anion gap is positive. Serum anion gap is normal. Which type of renal tubular acidosis does she most likely have?
questions.explanation: Type 1 (Distal) RTA is characterized by inability of the distal tubule to acidify urine, resulting in urine pH >5.5 despite systemic acidosis. Key features: normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, positive urine anion gap, and urine pH inappropriately alkaline. It is classically associated with Sjögren syndrome, SLE, and causes nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis. Type 4 RTA causes hyperkalemia. Type 2 RTA causes urine pH <5.5 once plasma HCO3 falls below threshold.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy develops cola-colored urine, facial puffiness, and hypertension 2 weeks after recovering from a sore throat. Urinalysis shows RBC casts and proteinuria. Serum C3 is low, C4 is normal. ASO titers are elevated. Renal biopsy shows diffuse endocapillary hypercellularity with subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy and granular IgG/C3 deposits on immunofluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN) classically presents 1-3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis with nephritic syndrome (hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, oliguria). Serological hallmark: low C3 with normal C4 (alternative complement pathway activation). Elevated ASO confirms prior streptococcal infection. Biopsy shows subepithelial 'humps' (immune complex deposits) — pathognomonic for PSGN. Most children recover completely without treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male underwent emergency surgery for a ruptured aortic aneurysm with intraoperative hypotension lasting 45 minutes. Post-operatively his urine output drops to 15 mL/hour. Urine sodium is 52 mEq/L, urine osmolality is 290 mOsm/kg, and urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. What is the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) value expected in this condition?
questions.explanation: This patient has ischemic Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) from prolonged intraoperative hypotension. ATN causes intrinsic renal AKI where tubular cells are damaged and cannot reabsorb sodium effectively, resulting in FENa >2% (classically >2%). Muddy brown granular casts are pathognomonic for ATN. Urine sodium is high (>40 mEq/L) and urine osmolality is isosthenuric (~300 mOsm/kg). This contrasts with pre-renal AKI where FENa <1% due to intact tubular function.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 6-year-old boy presents with failure to thrive, polyuria, and polydipsia. Laboratory investigations show: serum sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 2.4 mEq/L, chloride 88 mEq/L, bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, and normal blood pressure. Serum renin and aldosterone are both elevated. Urine chloride is high. No history of diuretic use or vomiting. Which tubular transporter is most likely defective?

options.A: Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) in distal convoluted tubule
options.B: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in thick ascending limb of Henle
options.C: Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in collecting duct

questions.explanation: Bartter syndrome is caused by defects in the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (or associated channels like ROMK, ClC-Kb). It presents with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, normal blood pressure (distinguishing from hyperaldosteronism), elevated renin and aldosterone, high urine chloride, and failure to thrive in childhood. It mimics chronic loop diuretic use. Gitelman syndrome affects NCC in DCT and presents later with hypomagnesemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male undergoes a cadaveric renal transplant. On post-operative day 7, he develops fever, graft tenderness, rising serum creatinine, and oliguria. Doppler ultrasound shows good vascular flow to the graft. Renal biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration of tubules (tubulitis) and interstitium with focal tubular injury. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial treatment?

options.B: Acute antibody-mediated rejection — plasmapheresis and IVIG
options.C: Acute T-cell mediated (cellular) rejection — high-dose IV methylprednisolone

questions.explanation: Acute cellular (T-cell mediated) rejection typically occurs within days to weeks post-transplant. Biopsy findings of tubulitis and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate are hallmarks (Banff classification Grade IA/IB). Treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy (500 mg-1g for 3 days). Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes (pre-formed antibodies). Antibody-mediated rejection shows C4d deposits and microvascular injury on biopsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male presents with massive proteinuria (8.2 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (2.1 g/dL), and bilateral leg edema. He has a history of hepatitis B infection. Renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial immune complex deposits forming a 'spike and dome' pattern on silver stain. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 deposits. Anti-PLA2R antibody is positive. Which of the following represents the most serious acute complication specific to this patient's proteinuria level?

options.B: Renal vein thrombosis with risk of pulmonary embolism
options.D: Bilateral pleural effusions causing respiratory failure

questions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy (MN) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. The 'spike and dome' pattern on silver stain with subepithelial deposits and positive anti-PLA2R antibody confirm primary MN. The most feared acute complication of nephrotic syndrome — particularly MN — is renal vein thrombosis, due to loss of anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin III, protein C and S) in urine, leading to a hypercoagulable state. This can extend to pulmonary embolism. Risk is highest when serum albumin <2.5 g/dL.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl presents with nephrotic syndrome and persistent microscopic hematuria. Serum C3 is persistently low over 8 weeks while C4 remains normal. Renal biopsy on electron microscopy shows dense intramembranous deposits (dense deposit disease). A serum autoantibody is detected that stabilizes the C3 convertase of the alternative complement pathway. Which autoantibody is responsible?
questions.explanation: Dense Deposit Disease (DDD), a subtype of C3 glomerulopathy (formerly MPGN type II), is characterized by persistent hypocomplementemia with low C3 and normal C4 (alternative pathway activation only). The pathogenic autoantibody is C3 Nephritic Factor (C3NeF) — an IgG autoantibody that binds and stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), preventing its normal decay and causing uncontrolled C3 consumption. EM showing electron-dense intramembranous ribbon-like deposits is pathognomonic.
